---
title: "Quiz: objects instead of pixels"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Name two questions that object-based colocalisation answers and pixel coefficients cannot.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Pixel coefficients give one number per region.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Which structures overlap (the share of A objects with a B partner, object by object), and how far apart partners are (a distance per pair, even below the resolution). Pixel coefficients mix all structures into one intensity-weighted number.
:::

---

**Q2.** Large A objects lie next to smaller B objects and touch them along one side. Which of "any overlap", "more than 50 % overlap" and "centroid in B" will report colocalisation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where is the centre of a large object that only touches its neighbour?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Only "any overlap": a few pixels of each A object are in a B object, far less than half, and the A centroid lies outside B. (Demo: 79 %, 0 % and 0 %.) With small A objects inside large B objects all three would agree.
:::

---

**Q3.** 40 % of the A spots have a B spot within 200 nm. Is that strong colocalisation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many B spots are there?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It depends on the density of B spots. With sparse B the chance level is a few per cent and 40 % is far above it; with dense B the chance level can be 30–50 %, and 40 % means nothing. Report the chance level (or the corrected fraction) next to the observed one.
:::

---

**Q4.** To build a null distribution, B spots are moved to random positions over the whole image instead of inside the cells. Which way does that bias the conclusion?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where do the relocated spots end up, and how far are they from A spots?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Many relocated B spots land outside the cells, far from every A spot, so the random arrangements show fewer close neighbours than any real unrelated arrangement in the cells. The chance level is underestimated and the real data look "attracted" even when they are not. Relocate inside the cell mask.
:::

---

**Q5.** Two-colour spots of the same molecule (true distance 0) are measured with 20 nm precision per channel. The average measured distance is 35 nm. Is the microscope misaligned?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Can a measured distance be negative?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not necessarily. The localisation errors of the two channels add up in the distance, and a distance is never negative, so the mean is biased upward: for $d = 0$ it is $\sqrt{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2}\sqrt{\pi/2} = 28.3 \times 1.25 \approx 35$ nm. A misalignment would show as a **consistent direction** of the separation vectors, not just as a mean distance.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why can centroids measure a 60 nm distance between two colours when the resolution is about 200 nm?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Resolution is about telling two points of the same colour apart.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The resolution limit concerns separating two unknown points in one image. Here each channel contains one spot, so we know which light belongs to which point, and the centre of each blurred spot can be found to a few nm with enough photons. The distance between the two centres is measurable, provided the channels are registered (chromatic shift) and the precision is reported.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* B spots are a Poisson process of density $\rho_B$. Show that the probability that a given A spot has no B spot within $d$ is $e^{-\rho_B\pi d^2}$, and compute the chance fraction within $d = 150$ nm for 2 B spots per µm².

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many B spots fall in a disc of area $\pi d^2$, and how is that number distributed?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The number of B spots in the disc is Poisson with mean $\rho_B\pi d^2$; the probability of zero is $e^{-\rho_B\pi d^2}$. With $\rho_B = 2$ µm⁻² and $d = 0.15$ µm: $\rho_B\pi d^2 = 2\pi \cdot 0.0225 = 0.141$, so the chance fraction is $1 - e^{-0.141} = 0.13$: 13 % of the A spots have a B spot within 150 nm by chance.
:::
